entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ⲕⲱⲧⲉ 'turn, go round' (ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲱⲧⲉ ⲙ̄- 'around'); G5117 (τόπος)
entries.partOfSpeech: prepositional phrase in a nominal sentence; imperative
entries.literal: that (one) is around the lamb; seek for yourselves a place within a repose
entries.standardEnglish: Translations often supply words: '(Why does) that man (carry) the lamb around?'
entries.wohChoice: Manuscript reading kept: 'That one is around the lamb.' No words are supplied. 'seek a place for yourselves within repose'.
entries.rationale: ⲡⲏ ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲱⲧⲉ ⲙ̄- is a complete Coptic nominal sentence ('that one is around …'), so the line can be printed as written, and the crux rule requires the manuscript reading where the difficulty is one of sense rather than grammar. The usual supplements turn the remark into a question about why the man carries the lamb, which fits the disciples' answer but adds words the manuscript does not have; they are given in the commentary. The final instruction uses τόπος and ἀνάπαυσις, rendered 'place' and 'repose' under their entries.

entries.strongs: Mk 15:40; 16:1 (Σαλώμη); Crum s.v. ⲡⲉⲕ- (feminine ⲧⲉⲕ-)
entries.literal: Salome; I am your (female) disciple
entries.standardEnglish: 'Salome'; Lambdin supplies a speech formula before 'I am your disciple'
entries.wohChoice: 'Salome', without further identification in the line. Her reply 'I am your disciple' carries no speech formula in the Coptic, and none is supplied in the English (register convention); the feminine ⲧⲉⲕ-, which identifies the speaker as Salome, is explained in the commentary.
entries.rationale: The name is spelled as in the Greek NT (Σαλώμη, Mk 15:40; 16:1), where a Salome is among the women at the cross and the tomb; Thomas does not say which Salome is meant, so the identification belongs in the commentary. In Coptic the possessive article ⲧⲉⲕ- is feminine and shows that the speaker of 'I am your disciple' is a woman, i.e. Salome; English cannot mark this in the pronoun, and the binding register convention forbids supplying a formula the Coptic lacks. The commentary therefore states the speaker explicitly, and the question whether an English ⟨Salome said:⟩ should be admitted is escalated for human review.

entries.partOfSpeech: relative statives; circumstantial statives; indefinite pronoun
entries.literal: as from someone; the one who exists from the one who is equal; when he is destroyed … when he is divided
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin: 'I am he who exists from the undivided'; emendation ϣⲏϣ for ϣⲏϥ (Layton 1989, p. 74, cited by Dilley)
entries.wohChoice: 'As though from someone' (indefinite ⲟⲩⲁ); 'the one who is equal' for ⲡⲉⲧϣⲏϣ (literal stative); manuscript ϣⲏϥ kept as 'When he is destroyed', 'divided' for ⲡⲏϣ.
entries.rationale: ϣⲏϣ is the stative of ϣⲱϣ 'be equal, level', so 'the one who is equal' is the literal meaning; Lambdin's 'the undivided' interprets it by contrast with ⲡⲏϣ 'divided' later in the saying, and that interpretation is given in the commentary. The manuscript's ϣⲏϥ (stative of ϣⲱϥ 'be desolate, destroyed') may be a slip for ϣⲏϣ, and Dilley's notes record both the suspicion of corruption and the conjectural emendation (Layton 1989, p. 74); the crux rule keeps the manuscript reading in the line and the emendation in the commentary. ⲟⲩⲁ without article is regularly the indefinite 'someone', which gives Salome's challenge a coherent sense (a stranger sharing her couch as if he were someone's guest); 'the One' would read a title into the indefinite pronoun.

entries.strongs: G3466 (μυστήριον); Crum s.v. ϣⲁ (ⲙ̄ⲡϣⲁ 'be worthy')
entries.literal: it is to those worthy of my mysteries that I tell my mysteries
entries.standardEnglish: 'mysteries' (standard); 'secrets' in some translations
entries.wohChoice: 'mysteries'. The focalising (second) present ⲉⲓ̈ϫⲱ is rendered as a cleft: 'It is to [those who are worthy] of [my] mysteries that I tell my mysteries.' (changed from the draft's uncleft order).
entries.rationale: μυστήριον is the word of Mk 4:11 ('the mystery of the kingdom') and is rendered 'mystery' in the standard English versions, so 'mysteries' keeps the synoptic resonance and is what the major translations of Thomas print. 'Secrets' would blur the link with the 'hidden' sayings of the incipit, which use a different, native word (ϩⲏⲡ). The corpus parses ⲉⲓ̈- as the focalising converter, which puts the emphasis on the adverbial phrase; English expresses that with a cleft, as Block A does for focalising forms (THOM-12) and Block B at THOM-49.

entries.literal: whoever knows the All, being in need himself, is in need of the whole place
entries.standardEnglish: 'If one who knows the all still feels a personal deficiency, he is completely deficient' and other parses (some take ⲟⲩⲁⲁϥ with 'the All')
entries.wohChoice: 'Whoever knows the All but is lacking in himself is lacking entirely.' ⲟⲩⲁⲁϥ is read with the circumstantial ('in himself'); ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲧⲏⲣϥ is read as the adverbial idiom 'entirely', so the topos/ma entry is not applied here.
entries.rationale: The saying turns on two uncertain points: whether ⲟⲩⲁⲁϥ ('alone, himself') qualifies the knower's lack or the All, and whether ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲧⲏⲣϥ ('the whole place') is literal or idiomatic. The adopted parse takes ⲟⲩⲁⲁϥ with the nearest verb, which is the simplest syntax, and reads ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲧⲏⲣϥ as an expression of totality, which gives the antithesis the saying evidently intends (knowing the All, lacking oneself, lacking everything); because other parses are defended and the idiom is not certain, the choice is `inferred`. The ⟨ϥ⟩ supplied by the edition is a single letter and is rendered silently; 'the All' follows `ptirf-the-all-reign-over-the-all-thomas-woh`.

entries.strongs: G1377 (διώκω); Crum s.v. ϩⲏⲧ 'heart', ϩⲏ 'belly', ⲟⲩⲱϣ 'wish, desire'
entries.literal: they will not find a place in the place where they persecuted you; persecuted within their heart; the belly of the one who desires
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin-type smoothing at 68 ('wherever you have been persecuted they will find no place'); 69b often 'so that the belly of him who desires will be filled'
entries.wohChoice: Literal at 68: 'and they will not find a place in the place where they have persecuted you' (subject left as the persecutors; both 'place' words kept). At 69: 'persecuted within their heart'; 'the belly of the one who desires will be filled' (active impersonal rendered as passive).
entries.rationale: Logion 68 is obscure and has been smoothed in different directions; the literal English keeps both τόπος and ⲙⲁ as 'place', as the topos entry requires, and keeps the third-person plural subject, which most naturally resumes the persecutors. In 69 ϩⲣⲁⲓ̈ ϩⲙ̄ⲡⲟⲩϩⲏⲧ is literally 'within their heart', and the English does not decide between inward persecution and persecution on account of the heart, which the commentary sets out. ⲡⲉⲧⲟⲩⲱϣ is 'the one who wishes / desires', and 'the one who desires' keeps the paradox of the Coptic rather than paraphrasing it as 'whoever is in need'.

entries.standardEnglish: Various conjectural completions of the lost end ('[except me]', '[again]')
entries.wohChoice: 'I will [destroy this] house, and no one will be able to build it …': ⲕⲱⲧ = 'build' (not 'rebuild'); the unrestored gap is '…'; no completion is printed.
entries.rationale: ⲕⲱⲧ is the ordinary verb 'build', and 'rebuild' would add a sense of restoration that the Coptic does not express, harmonising toward Mk 14:58 and Jn 2:19. The end of the line is lost, and the source edition does not restore it, so rule 3 of the restored-text convention prints '…' and the commentary reports the conjectures as conjectures. The restored verb and demonstrative are bracketed together as one span, as adjacent restored English words are elsewhere.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϣⲱⲛⲉ 'be sick; sickness'; ϫⲱⲧⲉ not identified by the Editor as an attested noun of this sense; emendation ϣⲱⲧⲉ 'well, cistern' (Layton 1989, p. 80, cited by Dilley); Origen, Contra Celsum 8.15-16 (the 'heavenly dialogue')
entries.literal: Lord, there are many around the ϫⲱⲧⲉ, but there is no one in the sickness
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin: 'O lord, there are many around the drinking trough, but there is nothing in the cistern' (emending ϣⲱⲛⲉ)
entries.wohChoice: Manuscript reading kept: 'Lord, there are many around the drinking trough(?), but there is no one in the sickness(?).' '(?)' on both nouns: ϫⲱⲧⲉ is of uncertain meaning, and ϣⲱⲛⲉ 'sickness' does not agree with its feminine article (see rationale). The emendation ϣⲱⲧⲉ 'well, cistern' is given in commentary.
entries.rationale: ϣⲱⲛⲉ is a common, securely attested Coptic word for 'sickness' (Crum s.v.; the same lemma appears in ⲛⲉⲧϣⲱⲛⲉ 'the sick' at THOM-14), so the manuscript reading is lexically clear even though it fits the image poorly; the widely printed 'well' or 'cistern' rests on the conjecture ϣⲱⲧⲉ, which Dilley records as uncertain, and on the Greek saying 'many around the well, no one in the well' reported by Origen (Contra Celsum 8.15-16). The crux rule keeps the manuscript in the line and the emendation in the commentary, and the '(?)' convention is reserved for a word whose meaning cannot be established: that is the case for ϫⲱⲧⲉ, for which 'drinking trough' (Lambdin) is a contextual guess. The vocative 'Lord' and the unnamed speaker ('He said') follow the Coptic. Ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01): the article in ⲧϣⲱⲛⲉ is feminine, but ϣⲱⲛⲉ 'sickness' is masculine (Crum, Coptic Dictionary 571a), while ϣⲱⲧⲉ 'pit, well, cistern' is feminine (Crum 595a); the article therefore supports the emendation, and 'sickness' carries '(?)'.

entries.strongs: Crum s.v. ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ 'bride' (ⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ 'bridal chamber'); cf. G3567 (νυμφών); Thomas 104 has the Greek loan ⲛⲩⲙⲫⲱⲛ
entries.literal: the place of the bride / of the wedding
entries.standardEnglish: 'the bridal chamber' (Lambdin and most translations); 'the wedding hall'
entries.wohChoice: 'the bridal chamber' (75); 'is going to be married' for ⲣ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ (64). ⲙⲁ here is part of a compound and is not rendered 'place'. When Block C reaches logion 104 (Greek ⲛⲩⲙⲫⲱⲛ), the loan/native pair is to be recorded there.
entries.rationale: ⲙⲁ ⲛ̄- + noun is a productive Coptic way of forming nouns of place, and ⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ is the native equivalent of Greek νυμφών 'bridal chamber, wedding hall' (Mt 9:15), so 'bridal chamber' is the standard and lexically exact rendering; a literal 'place of the bride' would make a compound look like a phrase. The English term is also the name of a later Valentinian rite (Gospel of Philip), and the commentary states that the rendering does not import that rite into Thomas, where the image is a wedding feast and the contrast is between the many at the door and the few who enter. ⲣ̄ϣⲉⲗⲉⲉⲧ 'be married' at 64 uses the same root, and the entry records the link.

entries.literal: a man, a merchant; cargo; he was wise; this single pearl; seek his treasure
entries.standardEnglish: Lambdin: 'a merchant who had a consignment of merchandise … That merchant was shrewd … seek his unfailing and enduring treasure'
entries.wohChoice: 'a man, a merchant'; 'merchandise' for ⲫⲟⲣⲧⲓⲟⲛ; 'wise' for ⲥⲁⲃⲉ; 'this single pearl' (adjectival ⲟⲩⲱⲧ, see the oua-ouot entry); 'his treasure': the possessive ⲉϥ, which Dilley's diplomatic text marks as editorial deletion {ⲉϥ}, is kept, with the normalised layer and Lambdin, because it is written in the manuscript and confirmed by the scribe's own correction.
entries.rationale: The appositive ⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛ̄ⲉϣⲱⲱⲧ ('a man, a merchant') is kept as the Coptic has it, under the ⲣⲱⲙⲉ entry; ⲫⲟⲣⲧⲓⲟⲛ is a 'load, cargo', and 'merchandise' renders it in the commercial sense the context requires. ⲥⲁⲃⲉ is the ordinary word for 'wise' and shares the English with ⲫⲣⲟⲛⲓⲙⲟⲥ (39) and ⲣⲙ̄ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧ (8); 'shrewd' would distinguish them but would add a nuance of calculation that ⲥⲁⲃⲉ does not carry, so the shared English is recorded here. At 'his treasure' the manuscript has ⲡⲉϥ- with an ⲉ written above the line, a correction that yields ⲡⲉϥⲉϩⲟ 'his treasure'; the curly brackets are the modern editor's judgement that the possessive is an error, so convention 6 (the manuscript reading stands) governs over the silent-drop rule for { }, and 'the treasure' is reported in the commentary.

entries.literal: is circumcision useful or not?; the true circumcision in spirit has found profit entirely
entries.standardEnglish: 'beneficial … profitable in every respect' (Lambdin-type); 'in the Spirit' in some translations

entries.rationale: The saying uses a Greek verb in the question and a native compound in the answer, and two English words keep that shift visible. 'In spirit' follows the ratified lower-case rule for ⲡⲛⲉⲩⲙⲁ, and the phrase recalls Rom 2:29 ('circumcision of the heart, in spirit'), where English versions also differ on the capital; the commentary notes the parallel without importing a reading. The central brit-milah entry documents the Hebrew covenant term of Gen 17 and its wohChoice governs Hebrew wording that Thomas does not share, so citing it would imply a lexical link that does not exist.
